angle: 15 assets that pay monthly, from 3 angles: numbers, psychology, playbook
title: 15 Assets That Pay You Every Month

scenes.text: Hi, I'm Ryan Rover. Imagine checking your bank account at the start of every month and seeing money arrive that you didn't work for that month. Not a paycheck. Not a side gig. Just income from things you own. That's what wealthy people mean when they talk about making their money work for them. Today I'll walk you through fifteen assets that can pay you every month, what they really pay, the traps to avoid and how to build your own monthly income machine.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Here's the core math. At a four percent yearly yield, one hundred thousand dollars produces about three hundred thirty three dollars a month. To earn one thousand dollars a month, you'd need roughly three hundred thousand dollars. At a six percent yield, about two hundred thousand. Higher yields need less money, but usually come with more risk.

card.note: yields change over time; illustrations, not promises

scenes.short_hook: How much money do you need to earn a thousand dollars a month without working?

scenes.text: That math is the key to everything in this video. Monthly income from assets is simply the amount you own multiplied by the yield, divided by twelve. So there are only two ways to get more monthly income. Own more, or earn a higher yield. And because higher yields almost always come with higher risk, the most reliable path is usually owning more, steadily, over time.
scenes.caption: OWN MORE OR EARN MORE

scenes.text: We'll go through these fifteen assets from three angles. First, the numbers. Five safer, cash like assets and what they actually pay. Second, the psychology. Five higher yield assets, and the mental traps that make people overpay for income. And third, the playbook. Five ownership assets and a step by step plan to build monthly income. Reminder, this is education, not financial advice. Rates and yields change constantly, so always check current numbers.
scenes.caption: THREE ANGLES

scenes.text: Let's start with the numbers. And the first asset is one almost everyone can open today.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Our numbers. Deposit insurance rules come from the FDIC and NCUA. Treasury information comes from TreasuryDirect and the U.S. Treasury. Fund information comes from the SEC and fund disclosures. Social Security rules come from the Social Security Administration. Yields mentioned are illustrations, because real rates change with the economy. This is education, not financial advice.
scenes.caption: OUR NUMBERS

scenes.text: Angle one. The numbers. Five safer assets that pay monthly, and what you can realistically expect from them.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Asset number one. A high yield savings account.
scenes.caption: ASSET 1

scenes.text: The simplest monthly paying asset is a high yield savings account. Most banks and credit unions pay interest monthly, and many online banks pay far more than traditional savings accounts. In recent years, many high yield accounts have paid several percent, while some big bank savings accounts paid close to zero.
scenes.caption: INTEREST EVERY MONTH

scenes.text: Money in a bank is typically protected by FDIC insurance, and at credit unions by NCUA insurance, up to two hundred fifty thousand dollars per depositor, per institution, per ownership category. That makes it one of the safest places for money you might need.
scenes.caption: INSURED UP TO $250,000

scenes.text: The downside is that rates can change at any time, and they usually fall when the Federal Reserve cuts interest rates. Over long periods, savings rates have often barely kept up with inflation, or fallen behind.
scenes.caption: RATES CAN DROP ANYTIME

scenes.text: So a high yield savings account is perfect for your emergency fund and short term goals, but usually not the best place for money you won't need for decades. It's a parking spot, not a growth engine.
scenes.caption: A PARKING SPOT

scenes.text: Here's what that means in dollars. On a twenty thousand dollar emergency fund, the difference between a rate near zero and a rate of four percent is roughly eight hundred dollars a year, or about sixty seven dollars a month. That's real money for doing nothing more than moving your savings to a better account at an insured bank. It's one of the easiest monthly raises you'll ever give yourself.
scenes.caption: ABOUT $67 A MONTH ON $20K

scenes.text: Try this. Compare your current savings rate with a few reputable online banks. If yours pays far less, moving your emergency fund could earn you real money every month with almost no extra risk.
scenes.caption: COMPARE YOUR RATE

scenes.text: Asset number two. Money market funds.
scenes.caption: ASSET 2

scenes.text: Money market funds are mutual funds that invest in very short term, high quality debt, like Treasury bills and commercial paper. They usually aim to keep a stable value of one dollar per share and pay dividends that are typically credited monthly.
scenes.caption: STABLE $1 SHARE, MONTHLY DIVIDENDS

scenes.text: Their yields usually move closely with short term interest rates. When rates were high in recent years, many money market funds paid yields similar to or above high yield savings accounts.
scenes.caption: YIELDS FOLLOW SHORT RATES

scenes.text: One important difference is that money market funds are not FDIC insured. They're considered very low risk, but not risk free. A few have fallen below one dollar per share in rare crises, such as 2008.
scenes.caption: NOT FDIC INSURED

scenes.text: Government money market funds, which invest mostly in U.S. Treasury securities, are generally considered among the safest. Some also generate income that's exempt from state income taxes, depending on holdings and your state.
scenes.caption: GOVERNMENT FUNDS ARE SAFEST

scenes.text: Money market funds are also extremely convenient. They usually sit right inside your brokerage account, so you can move money between them and your investments in a day or two. Many investors use them as a holding place for cash they plan to invest soon, or for the cash part of a retirement portfolio. The monthly dividends simply accumulate, or can be paid out to your bank.
scenes.caption: CONVENIENT AND FLEXIBLE

scenes.text: Try this. Check what your brokerage does with uninvested cash. Some pay very little on cash by default, while their money market funds pay much more. Moving idle cash can be an easy upgrade.
scenes.caption: CHECK YOUR IDLE CASH

scenes.text: Asset number three. A Treasury bill ladder.
scenes.caption: ASSET 3

scenes.text: Treasury bills are short term loans to the U.S. government, maturing in anywhere from a few weeks to one year. They're backed by the full faith and credit of the United States, which is why they're often considered one of the safest investments in the world.
scenes.caption: BACKED BY THE U.S. GOVERNMENT
scenes.short_hook: The U.S. government will pay you interest. Here's how to get it every month.

scenes.text: T bills don't pay monthly interest. You buy them at a discount and receive the full value at maturity. But you can create monthly income by building a ladder, buying bills that mature in different months so money comes back to you regularly.
scenes.caption: BUILD A LADDER

scenes.text: Interest on Treasury bills is subject to federal income tax, but exempt from state and local income taxes. For people in high tax states, that can make them more attractive than similar bank yields.
scenes.caption: NO STATE INCOME TAX

scenes.text: You can buy T bills directly through TreasuryDirect or through most brokerage accounts, often with no fees. Many brokerages also offer automatic rollover, so maturing bills are reinvested.
scenes.caption: BUY DIRECT OR AT A BROKER

scenes.text: Here's how a simple monthly ladder can work. Say you have twelve thousand dollars. You buy one thousand dollars of T bills maturing each month for the next year. Every month, one thousand dollars plus interest comes back. You can spend it, or buy a new twelve month bill to keep the ladder going. It's a simple way to turn the safest investment in the world into a monthly cash flow.
scenes.caption: A SIMPLE 12 MONTH LADDER

scenes.text: Try this. If you have cash you won't need for a few months, compare the current yield on a three month T bill with your savings account.
scenes.caption: COMPARE THE YIELD

scenes.text: Asset number four. Certificates of deposit with monthly interest.
scenes.caption: ASSET 4

scenes.text: A certificate of deposit, or CD, is a bank deposit where you agree to leave your money for a set period, like six months, a year or five years, in exchange for a fixed interest rate. Many banks let you choose to receive interest monthly.
scenes.caption: A FIXED RATE FOR A FIXED TIME

scenes.text: The advantage is certainty. If rates fall, your CD keeps paying the rate you locked in. And CDs at insured banks are covered by FDIC insurance within the limits.
scenes.caption: LOCK IN THE RATE

scenes.text: The downside is that withdrawing early usually triggers a penalty, often several months of interest. And if rates rise, you're stuck with your lower rate until the CD matures.
scenes.caption: EARLY WITHDRAWAL PENALTIES

scenes.text: A CD ladder, with CDs maturing at different times, gives you regular access to some of your money while capturing higher rates on longer terms.
scenes.caption: A CD LADDER

scenes.text: Some banks also offer no penalty CDs, which let you withdraw early without a penalty, usually at a slightly lower rate. And brokered CDs, bought through a brokerage account, can be sold before maturity on a secondary market, though their price can rise or fall. Each type trades a bit of yield for a bit of flexibility, so choose based on how sure you are about when you'll need the money.
scenes.caption: NO PENALTY AND BROKERED CDS

scenes.text: Try this. If you're saving for a specific goal one to three years away, like a car or a down payment, compare CD rates with your savings account.
scenes.caption: MATCH CDS TO GOALS

scenes.text: Asset number five. Bond funds.
scenes.caption: ASSET 5

scenes.text: Bond funds hold many bonds at once, from governments, companies or municipalities. Many bond funds and ETFs pay distributions monthly, from the interest their bonds earn.
scenes.caption: MANY BONDS, MONTHLY INCOME

scenes.text: Unlike CDs, bond fund prices move. When interest rates rise, existing bonds lose value, and bond fund prices fall. In 2022, as rates rose quickly, many bond funds had one of their worst years on record.
scenes.caption: PRICES MOVE WITH RATES

scenes.text: Duration measures how sensitive a bond fund is to interest rate changes. Short term bond funds usually move less. Long term bond funds can move a lot.
scenes.caption: KNOW THE DURATION

scenes.text: Municipal bond funds can pay income that's free from federal income tax, and sometimes state tax too. They can be useful for people in higher tax brackets investing in taxable accounts.
scenes.caption: MUNICIPAL BONDS

scenes.text: Bond funds earn their place in a portfolio by doing something stocks don't. In many stock market crashes, high quality government bonds have held their value or even risen, cushioning the fall. Not always, as 2022 showed, but often. That's why many retirees hold bond funds not just for their monthly income, but as a stabilizer that makes the whole portfolio easier to live with.
scenes.caption: A STABILIZER

scenes.text: Try this. If you own a bond fund, look up its duration and its credit quality. Those two numbers tell you most of what you need to know about its risk.
scenes.caption: CHECK DURATION AND QUALITY

scenes.text: That's angle one. High yield savings, money market funds, Treasury bills, CDs and bond funds. Safer assets with modest monthly income. Now angle two. Higher yields, and the psychology that gets people in trouble.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: As yields go up, so does risk, and so do the mental traps. Monthly income feels wonderful, and that feeling can push people into investments they don't fully understand. Here are five higher yield assets, each with a psychological lesson.
scenes.caption: HIGHER YIELD, MORE TRAPS

scenes.text: Asset number six. Monthly dividend stocks and ETFs.
scenes.caption: ASSET 6

scenes.text: Most U.S. companies that pay dividends pay them quarterly, but some pay monthly. One well known example is Realty Income, a real estate company that calls itself The Monthly Dividend Company. There are also ETFs that collect dividends from many companies and pay monthly.
scenes.caption: SOME PAY MONTHLY

scenes.text: Here's the psychological trap. People love monthly payments, so they sometimes choose investments just because they pay monthly, even if they're more expensive or riskier than quarterly payers. The payment schedule doesn't change the total return.
scenes.caption: MONTHLY ISN'T BETTER BY ITSELF

scenes.text: Remember also that dividends aren't free money. When a company pays a dividend, its share price typically drops by roughly the dividend amount on the ex dividend date. What matters is total return, dividends plus price changes.
scenes.query: Stock price dropping on ex dividend date
scenes.caption: DIVIDENDS AREN'T FREE MONEY

scenes.text: Dividends can also be cut. During tough times, many companies have reduced or suspended dividends. A dividend is a decision by the company's board, not a promise.
scenes.caption: DIVIDENDS CAN BE CUT

scenes.text: There's also a concentration trap. Some people build a portfolio of only a handful of high yield dividend stocks, often clustered in the same few industries, like utilities, energy or real estate. If that sector struggles, much of their income can shrink at once. A diversified dividend fund spreads that risk across many companies and industries, so no single cut hurts too much.
scenes.caption: DON'T CONCENTRATE FOR YIELD

scenes.text: Try this. Before buying any dividend investment, look at its total return over ten years, not just its yield. A high yield with poor total return is a warning sign.
scenes.caption: CHECK TOTAL RETURN

scenes.text: Asset number seven. Real estate investment trusts.

card.title: REITs
card.sub: real estate income without the landlord

scenes.caption: ASSET 7

scenes.text: REITs are companies that own or finance income producing real estate, like apartments, warehouses, offices or shopping centers. By law, to keep their special tax status, REITs generally must distribute at least ninety percent of their taxable income to shareholders.
scenes.caption: 90% PAYOUT REQUIREMENT

scenes.text: That's why REITs often have higher yields than average stocks. Some pay monthly, and REIT index funds give you diversified exposure to many properties at once.
scenes.caption: HIGHER YIELDS

scenes.text: The psychological trap with REITs is assuming real estate is always safe. REIT prices can fall sharply, especially when interest rates rise or a property type struggles. Office REITs, for example, faced serious challenges as remote work spread.
scenes.caption: REAL ESTATE ISN'T ALWAYS SAFE

scenes.text: REIT dividends are often taxed as ordinary income rather than at lower qualified dividend rates, so many investors hold REITs in tax advantaged accounts like IRAs.
scenes.caption: TAX CONSIDERATIONS

scenes.text: REITs also have a useful feature for monthly income seekers. They trade like stocks, so you can buy as little as one share, or even a fraction, and sell any business day. Compare that with a rental property, which might take months and thousands of dollars in fees to sell. For many people, that liquidity makes REITs a far easier way to add real estate income to a portfolio.
scenes.caption: LIQUID REAL ESTATE

scenes.text: Try this. If you want real estate income without being a landlord, compare a low cost REIT index fund with individual REITs. The index fund spreads your risk across many property types.
scenes.caption: CONSIDER A REIT INDEX FUND

scenes.text: Asset number eight. Rental property.
scenes.caption: ASSET 8

scenes.text: Rental property is the classic monthly income asset. Tenants pay rent every month, and after expenses and mortgage payments, the leftover cash flow is yours. Over time, rents may rise and the mortgage shrinks.
scenes.caption: RENT EVERY MONTH

scenes.text: The psychological trap is focusing on gross rent instead of net cash flow. Property taxes, insurance, repairs, vacancies, maintenance and management fees can consume a large share of rent. Many new landlords discover their real profit is much smaller than they expected.
scenes.caption: GROSS RENT ISN'T PROFIT

scenes.text: Rental income is also not passive for most people. Finding tenants, handling repairs and dealing with problems takes time. Hiring a property manager helps, but it reduces your income.
scenes.caption: NOT REALLY PASSIVE

scenes.text: On the positive side, rental property offers leverage, potential appreciation and tax benefits like depreciation. For the right person, it can be a powerful monthly income source.
scenes.caption: POWERFUL FOR THE RIGHT PERSON

scenes.text: Here's a rough illustration. A property renting for two thousand dollars a month might have a mortgage of one thousand two hundred, property taxes and insurance of three hundred, and a repair and vacancy reserve of three hundred. That leaves about two hundred dollars a month of cash flow. Not huge, but it can grow as rents rise and the mortgage is eventually paid off. The real wealth often comes over decades.
scenes.caption: $2,000 RENT, ABOUT $200 CASH FLOW

scenes.text: Try this. Before buying a rental, estimate your net cash flow using conservative numbers, including at least one month of vacancy per year and a repair budget.
scenes.caption: USE CONSERVATIVE NUMBERS

scenes.text: Quick pause. If you're starting to picture your own monthly income machine, please subscribe to Ryan Rover Money. It's free, and it helps us keep making these. Now, asset number nine.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Asset number nine. Covered call ETFs.
scenes.caption: ASSET 9

scenes.text: Covered call ETFs own stocks and sell call options on them, collecting option premiums. Those premiums can create very high yields, often paid monthly, which makes these funds popular with income investors.
scenes.caption: HIGH YIELDS, OFTEN MONTHLY
scenes.short_hook: That fund paying ten percent a year has a hidden cost most people miss.

scenes.text: Here's the catch. By selling call options, these funds give up much of the upside when stocks rise sharply. In strong markets, they can lag far behind a regular index fund, while still taking most of the losses when markets fall.
scenes.caption: CAPPED UPSIDE, FULL DOWNSIDE

scenes.text: The psychological trap is yield fixation. A big yield feels like a big return. But some covered call funds have delivered lower total returns than simple index funds over time, even with their high monthly payments.
scenes.caption: YIELD ISN'T RETURN

scenes.text: Part of a high distribution can also come from returning your own capital, rather than true income. That can slowly shrink your investment.
scenes.caption: RETURN OF CAPITAL

scenes.text: Covered call funds can still have a place. Some retirees value a smoother, higher monthly payout more than maximum growth, and accept lagging in strong bull markets in exchange. That's a reasonable choice, as long as it's a choice made with open eyes. The problem is only when people buy them believing a high yield means a high return with no trade off.
scenes.caption: A CHOICE, WITH OPEN EYES

scenes.text: Try this. Before buying a covered call fund, compare its total return with a plain index fund over five or ten years. Then decide whether the steady income is worth the trade off.
scenes.caption: COMPARE TOTAL RETURNS

scenes.text: Asset number ten. Income annuities.
scenes.caption: ASSET 10

scenes.text: A simple income annuity, sometimes called a single premium immediate annuity, works like buying a pension. You give an insurance company a lump sum, and it pays you a fixed amount every month for life, or for a set period.
scenes.caption: BUY YOURSELF A PENSION

scenes.text: The big benefit is protection against outliving your money. No matter how long you live, the checks keep coming, backed by the insurer. Economists have long noted that annuities can be valuable, yet relatively few retirees buy them, sometimes called the annuity puzzle.
scenes.caption: PROTECTION AGAINST LONG LIFE

scenes.text: The psychological barrier is the fear of dying early and losing the money. That fear is real, but some annuities offer guaranteed periods or refunds to heirs, at the cost of lower payments.
scenes.caption: THE FEAR OF LOSING OUT

scenes.text: Be careful. Many complex annuities have high fees, surrender charges and confusing terms. Simple income annuities are usually easier to understand. Payments generally aren't inflation adjusted unless you pay for that feature, and they depend on the insurer's strength.
scenes.caption: BEWARE COMPLEX ANNUITIES

scenes.text: Here's how annuity payments generally work. The older you are when you buy, the higher the monthly payment, because the insurer expects to pay for fewer years. Payments also depend on interest rates at the time you buy. That's why some retirees buy annuities in stages over several years, rather than all at once, to spread out their timing.
scenes.caption: OLDER BUYERS GET MORE

scenes.text: Try this. If you're near retirement, ask a fee only fiduciary planner whether covering basic expenses with Social Security plus a simple annuity makes sense for you.
scenes.caption: ASK A FIDUCIARY

scenes.text: That's angle two. Monthly dividend stocks, REITs, rental property, covered call ETFs and income annuities. Higher yields with real trade offs. Now angle three. The playbook.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: The final five assets are about ownership and long term strategy, plus a plan to combine everything into reliable monthly income. Some of these take years to build, but they can become the strongest income sources of all. And unlike the safer assets in angle one, several of them can grow their payments over time, which is exactly what you need to keep up with inflation over a long retirement.
scenes.caption: OWNERSHIP AND STRATEGY

scenes.text: Asset number eleven. A staggered dividend portfolio.
scenes.caption: ASSET 11

scenes.text: Most dividend stocks and index funds pay quarterly. But because different companies pay in different months, a diversified portfolio can produce income almost every month.
scenes.caption: QUARTERLY BECOMES MONTHLY

scenes.text: A broad dividend index fund, or simply a total market index fund, gives you dividends from hundreds of companies. Many investors also hold cash reserves to smooth out the months with smaller payments.
scenes.caption: BROAD FUNDS WORK

scenes.text: Some retirees simply set up a fixed monthly withdrawal from their portfolio, combining dividends and small sales. That creates a steady paycheck, regardless of when dividends arrive.
scenes.caption: CREATE YOUR OWN PAYCHECK

scenes.text: Focusing on dividend growth rather than high yield can help income rise over time. Companies with long records of raising dividends often have strong businesses, though past increases don't guarantee future ones.
scenes.caption: DIVIDEND GROWTH

scenes.text: Here's an example of the math. A diversified stock index fund yielding around one and a half percent pays far less monthly income than a high yield fund. But over long periods, its growth has often been much stronger. Many retirees combine a modest dividend with small regular sales, creating a sustainable paycheck while keeping the growth engine running.
scenes.caption: DIVIDENDS PLUS GROWTH

scenes.text: Try this. Look at your brokerage's dividend calendar to see when your investments pay. You may already have more monthly income than you realize.
scenes.caption: CHECK YOUR CALENDAR

scenes.text: Asset number twelve. A small business.
scenes.caption: ASSET 12

scenes.text: A profitable small business can pay its owner every month. Some business owners eventually hire managers, so the business runs without them being there every day, turning it into a true income asset.
scenes.caption: OWNER INCOME

scenes.text: Businesses with recurring revenue, like subscriptions, service contracts or maintenance plans, are especially valuable, because they produce predictable monthly income.
scenes.caption: RECURRING REVENUE

scenes.text: But businesses take work, money and risk to build, and many fail. Most owners spend years working hard before income becomes even partly passive.
scenes.caption: IT TAKES WORK

scenes.text: Some people buy existing businesses with steady cash flow instead of starting from scratch. That still requires careful research, and often financing.
scenes.caption: BUY OR BUILD

scenes.text: The real value of a business often shows up when it's sold. Small businesses frequently sell for a few times their yearly profit. So a business that pays its owner fifty thousand dollars a year could also be worth one hundred to two hundred thousand dollars to a buyer. That's a double benefit, monthly income now and a valuable asset later.
scenes.caption: INCOME NOW, VALUE LATER

scenes.text: Try this. Think about skills you already have that people pay for monthly, like lawn care, bookkeeping or tutoring. Recurring services can grow into a real business.
scenes.caption: START WITH RECURRING SERVICES

scenes.text: Asset number thirteen. Royalties and digital products.
scenes.caption: ASSET 13

scenes.text: Books, music, online courses, templates, stock photos and apps can earn money long after they're created. Many platforms pay creators monthly.
scenes.caption: CREATE ONCE, EARN REPEATEDLY

scenes.text: The appeal is scalability. Selling one more digital copy costs almost nothing. A successful product can earn for years.
scenes.caption: SCALABLE INCOME

scenes.text: The reality is that most creative products earn very little. It often takes many products, consistent marketing and years of effort before income becomes meaningful.
scenes.caption: MOST EARN LITTLE

scenes.text: Treat it like planting seeds. Each product is a small seed. Most stay small, but a few can grow into steady monthly income.
scenes.caption: PLANT MANY SEEDS

scenes.text: Traditional royalties exist too. Authors earn royalties from book sales, musicians from streams and licensing, and some investors even buy existing royalty streams on specialized marketplaces. These can produce monthly payments, but they often decline over time as a song or book gets older, so they're best treated as a bonus, not a foundation.
scenes.caption: ROYALTIES OFTEN FADE

scenes.text: Try this. If you have knowledge people want, create one small digital product, like a guide or template, and see whether anyone buys it.
scenes.caption: CREATE ONE SMALL PRODUCT

scenes.text: Asset number fourteen. A paid off home.

card.title: A paid off home
card.sub: income you don't have to pay

scenes.caption: ASSET 14

scenes.text: A paid off home doesn't send you a check, but it does something similar. It removes one of the biggest monthly expenses most people have. Every month without a mortgage payment is money that stays in your pocket.
scenes.caption: NO MORTGAGE PAYMENT
scenes.short_hook: The most underrated monthly income asset might be the roof over your head.

scenes.text: Economists call the value of living in a home you own imputed rent. You're effectively paying rent to yourself. For retirees, a paid off home can dramatically lower how much income they need.
scenes.caption: IMPUTED RENT

scenes.text: You still pay property taxes, insurance and maintenance, so it's not free. But those costs are usually much lower than a full mortgage or rent payment.
scenes.caption: STILL SOME COSTS

scenes.text: Whether to pay off a mortgage early depends on your interest rate and other goals. A low rate mortgage might be fine to keep while you invest, while a high rate mortgage might be worth paying down faster.
scenes.caption: IT DEPENDS ON YOUR RATE

scenes.text: A paid off home also gives you options. Some retirees downsize and invest the difference. Others use a reverse mortgage, a loan that lets homeowners sixty two and older convert part of their home equity into income, though these come with costs and rules that deserve careful review. And for many, simply having no housing payment is the greatest financial peace of mind there is.
scenes.caption: A PAID OFF HOME CREATES OPTIONS

scenes.text: Try this. Calculate how much lower your monthly expenses would be without a mortgage. That number shows how much income a paid off home is worth to you.
scenes.caption: CALCULATE ITS VALUE

scenes.text: Asset number fifteen. Delayed Social Security.
scenes.caption: ASSET 15

scenes.text: Social Security pays monthly for life and adjusts for inflation, features that would be expensive to buy privately. For many people, it's their most valuable monthly income asset.
scenes.caption: MONTHLY, FOR LIFE, INFLATION ADJUSTED

scenes.text: You can claim as early as sixty two, but benefits are permanently reduced. For each year you delay past full retirement age, up to age seventy, benefits increase by about eight percent, according to the Social Security Administration.
scenes.caption: ABOUT 8% MORE PER YEAR OF DELAY

scenes.text: Delaying isn't right for everyone. Health, other savings and marriage all matter. But for many people, especially those who expect to live long, delaying can significantly increase lifetime income.
scenes.caption: NOT RIGHT FOR EVERYONE

scenes.text: Some retirees use savings to cover the years between retirement and claiming Social Security, effectively buying a larger lifetime income.
scenes.caption: BRIDGE TO A BIGGER CHECK

scenes.text: Here's an example. Someone with a full retirement age benefit of two thousand dollars a month might receive roughly one thousand four hundred dollars if they claim at sixty two, and roughly two thousand four hundred eighty at seventy, if their full retirement age is sixty seven. That's a difference of more than one thousand dollars a month, for life, adjusted for inflation.
scenes.caption: $1,400 VS $2,480 A MONTH

scenes.text: Try this. Check your Social Security statement to see your estimated monthly benefit at sixty two, full retirement age and seventy.
scenes.caption: CHECK YOUR OPTIONS

scenes.text: Now let's put it all together. Here's how many people build monthly income in layers, from safest to riskiest.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Layer one is your emergency fund, in a high yield savings account or money market fund. It pays a little monthly interest, but its real job is protecting everything else. Without it, an unexpected bill can force you to sell investments at a bad time.
scenes.caption: LAYER 1: EMERGENCY FUND

scenes.text: Layer two is guaranteed income, like Social Security, a pension or a simple annuity. This covers your most basic expenses, so a market crash never threatens your ability to pay for food and housing.
scenes.caption: LAYER 2: GUARANTEED INCOME

scenes.text: Layer three is your diversified investment portfolio, stock and bond index funds, producing dividends, interest and growth. This covers lifestyle expenses and protects against inflation over decades.
scenes.caption: LAYER 3: DIVERSIFIED PORTFOLIO

scenes.text: Layer four is optional ownership income, like rental property, a business or royalties. These can add a lot, but they come with more work and risk.
scenes.caption: LAYER 4: OWNERSHIP INCOME

scenes.text: Here's a simple example of the layers working together. A retired couple spends five thousand dollars a month. Social Security covers three thousand two hundred. Their diversified portfolio of about five hundred forty thousand dollars, withdrawn at four percent, covers about one thousand eight hundred more. Their emergency fund sits in a money market fund. Every layer has a job, and no single asset has to carry the whole load.
scenes.caption: EVERY LAYER HAS A JOB

scenes.text: In your twenties and thirties, monthly income from assets is mostly about planting. Your emergency fund earns a little interest, and your retirement accounts reinvest every dividend automatically. You probably don't need the income yet, so letting it compound is usually the smartest move. Every dividend reinvested now becomes a bigger dividend later.
scenes.caption: 20s AND 30s: PLANT AND REINVEST

scenes.text: In your forties and fifties, many people start shaping their future income. Paying down the mortgage, checking Social Security estimates, maybe adding a rental property or building a business. This is when you decide which layers you'll rely on, and start building them on purpose.
scenes.caption: 40s AND 50s: SHAPE THE LAYERS

scenes.text: In your sixties and beyond, the focus shifts from growing assets to drawing income from them. Deciding when to claim Social Security, whether an annuity makes sense, how much to keep in cash and bonds, and setting up a steady monthly paycheck from your portfolio.
scenes.caption: 60s AND BEYOND: DRAW THE INCOME

scenes.text: Imagine two investors, each with three hundred thousand dollars, each wanting monthly income. The first chases the highest yields they can find, putting everything into a few funds paying ten or twelve percent. For a while, the monthly checks feel amazing.
scenes.caption: INVESTOR ONE CHASES YIELD
scenes.short_hook: Two investors wanted monthly income. One chased yield. One built a system.

scenes.text: But over time, some of those funds cut their payouts, and their share prices slowly fall. The income shrinks, and so does the principal. The high yield turned out to be partly their own money coming back to them.
scenes.caption: THE YIELD TRAP

scenes.text: The second investor builds layers. An emergency fund, a diversified portfolio yielding a more modest amount, and a plan to withdraw a sustainable percentage. Their income starts smaller but grows over time, and their principal stays intact.
scenes.caption: INVESTOR TWO BUILDS LAYERS

scenes.text: Ten years later, the difference is striking. The first investor's monthly checks are smaller than when they started, and their account is worth less than the original three hundred thousand. The second investor's income has grown with their dividends and withdrawals, and their portfolio is likely worth more than they put in. Same starting money. One chased a number. The other built a system that could last.
scenes.query: Two account balances after ten years
scenes.caption: TEN YEARS LATER

scenes.text: Question one. What's the safest monthly income asset? Insured bank accounts and CDs within FDIC or NCUA limits, and U.S. Treasury bills, are generally considered the safest. They also tend to pay the least over long periods.
scenes.caption: THE SAFEST OPTIONS

scenes.text: Question two. Is a high yield always a red flag? Not always, but it's a reason to look closer. Ask where the yield comes from, whether it's sustainable and what the total return has been.
scenes.caption: IS HIGH YIELD A RED FLAG?

scenes.text: Question three. How much do I need for passive income to replace my salary? Divide your yearly spending by a sustainable withdrawal or yield rate. At four percent, sixty thousand dollars a year needs about one point five million dollars, before considering Social Security or other income.
scenes.caption: REPLACING A SALARY

scenes.text: Question four. Should I reinvest my monthly income or spend it? If you don't need it yet, reinvesting usually builds more future income, because each payment buys more income producing assets. If you're retired and rely on it, spending it is exactly the point. Many people reinvest during their working years and switch to taking the income in retirement.
scenes.caption: REINVEST OR SPEND?

scenes.text: Question five. How are these income sources taxed? It varies a lot. Interest is usually taxed as ordinary income, qualified dividends often get lower rates, Treasury interest skips state tax, municipal bond interest may skip federal tax, and Roth withdrawals can be tax free. Where you hold each asset can matter as much as which asset you hold.
scenes.caption: HOW IS IT TAXED?

scenes.text: Question six. Can I build monthly income with a small amount of money? Yes, just slowly. Even a few thousand dollars in a high yield savings account or a dividend fund starts producing a little income. The amounts feel tiny at first, but every dollar you add, and every payment you reinvest, makes the next month's income a bit bigger. That's how every large income portfolio started.
scenes.caption: STARTING SMALL

scenes.text: Mistake one. Chasing the highest yield. Unusually high yields often signal higher risk, unsustainable payouts or a return of your own capital. Always ask where the yield comes from and how the total return has looked over many years.
scenes.caption: MISTAKE 1: CHASING YIELD

scenes.text: Mistake two. Putting everything in one income source. One property, one stock or one fund can disappoint. Spreading income across several layers, like Social Security, a diversified portfolio and cash, makes your monthly income much more reliable.
scenes.caption: MISTAKE 2: ONE SOURCE

scenes.text: Mistake three. Forgetting inflation. A fixed monthly payment that feels comfortable today can buy much less in twenty years. Include assets that can grow, like stocks, and income that adjusts for inflation, like Social Security.
scenes.caption: MISTAKE 3: FORGETTING INFLATION

scenes.text: Mistake four. Ignoring fees and fine print. Some income products charge high yearly fees or surrender charges that quietly eat into your monthly payments. Read the costs before you buy, and favor simple, low cost options.
scenes.caption: MISTAKE 4: FEES AND FINE PRINT

scenes.text: Quick recap. Angle one, the numbers. High yield savings, money market funds, Treasury bills, CDs and bond funds. These are the safer assets that pay modest monthly income and protect your short term money.
scenes.caption: THE NUMBERS: 1 TO 5

scenes.text: Angle two, the psychology. Monthly dividend stocks, REITs, rental property, covered call ETFs and income annuities. Higher yields, with real trade offs, and mental traps like yield fixation and the fear of spending.
scenes.caption: THE PSYCHOLOGY: 6 TO 10

scenes.text: Angle three, the playbook. A staggered dividend portfolio, a small business, royalties, a paid off home and delayed Social Security. Ownership assets that can grow, combined into layers that make your monthly income reliable for decades.
scenes.caption: THE PLAYBOOK: 11 TO 15

scenes.text: Monthly income from assets isn't magic. It's ownership multiplied by time. Start with the safe layers, avoid the yield traps and keep adding to what you own. If you want my full step by step plan, it's in my playbook, linked in the description. Tell me in the comments, which of these fifteen assets do you already own? I'm Ryan Rover. See you in the next one.
scenes.caption: RYAN
